Lindsay Clancy jury split as holdout dispute raises mistrial risk
A juror dispute over reasonable doubt jolted Lindsay Clancy's murder trial after days of deadlock. The clash raises the prospect of a mistrial in a closely watched case centred on postpartum psychosis.
A jury in the trial of Lindsay Clancy went home without a verdict on Thursday after a sixth day of deliberations that took a dramatic turn, with the foreperson telling the judge that one juror would not follow the court's instructions on reasonable doubt. The jury is due to return on Friday to continue trying to reach a decision on whether the Massachusetts mother is criminally responsible for the deaths of her three children.
The development came as the defence asked the judge to remove a juror after heated discussions in court, a request that was rejected. Clancy, a 36-year-old former labour and delivery nurse, does not deny strangling her children in the basement of the family's home in 2023 before trying to take her own life. Her lawyer says postpartum psychosis drove her actions, while prosecutors say she knew what she was doing when she killed Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy, aged 5, 3 and 8 months.
Details of what happened in the jury room were not disclosed by the judge and were discussed only briefly in open court, but the note raised the possibility that a single holdout juror could be blocking a verdict. The trial, which has been livestreamed, has drawn heavy public attention, with reporters and spectators filling the courtroom, and has also led to debate over Clancy's culpability and maternal mental health after childbirth.
The jury had already twice told the judge it could not agree on a verdict, but Thursday marked the first sign of possible tension inside the deliberation room. Clancy's lawyer Kevin Reddington told the court that the foreperson had complained that one juror was refusing to listen to the law on reasonable doubt. After receiving the note, Judge William Sullivan called each juror in one by one and questioned them privately. He then repeated his instructions on reasonable doubt and sent them back to continue deliberating.
Reddington told the judge the juror should have been dismissed. "If we come back here in a half-hour with a mistrial because of a juror that has just spurned the instructions of this court, it's a shame - it's a real shame," he said, referring to the possibility of a deadlocked jury. Outside the courthouse later, he said the juror would be questioned again on Friday and added, "There's a person who has doubt but will not listen to the judge's instructions." Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said Sullivan's response was appropriate and that no further action was needed.
Sullivan said removing a juror during deliberations was a sensitive step. "I don't feel it is proper for me to side with one side or the other of the deliberations," the judge said. "I don't feel it's appropriate for me to say, 'I agree with one juror or the 11.' I have asked if they are able to follow my instructions. They swore earlier that they could." At one point, for the first time during the trial, Clancy was brought to a sidebar with the judge. Paralysed from the waist down after her suicide attempt, she uses a wheelchair, which Reddington pushed to the front of the courtroom. "She has a right to know what's going on," he later told reporters.
Signs of a possible hung jury had surfaced on Wednesday when Sullivan told the courtroom that jurors were stuck for a second time. He instructed them not to give up their own convictions simply to reach a verdict, but asked them to seriously consider opposing views and reassess their positions if appropriate. If the jury cannot agree, the judge could declare a mistrial. Prosecutors would then have to decide whether to try Clancy again, drop the charges or seek a plea deal.
If jurors find Clancy criminally responsible, they could convict her of murder or manslaughter. If she is acquitted, a judge could still order her to be confined to a mental health facility if an evaluation finds she poses a danger to the public. Reddington said on Thursday that Clancy has received letters of support "from all over the world" and added, "It's just amazing. She reads them all."
Jurors have heard evidence from relatives and doctors about Clancy's declining mental health in the months before the killings, including treatment with several medicines and a short stay in a psychiatric hospital. Experts called by the prosecution and the defence gave sharply different views on her psychiatric condition at the time of the killings. Patrick Clancy has said in interviews that he forgives his now ex-wife and sees her as ill, not evil. The defence says Clancy heard a voice telling her to kill the children so she could end her own life. Prosecutors say she deliberately sent her then husband out on errands to get him out of the house and have questioned how serious her suicide attempt was.
As the jury prepares to return on Friday, the case remains unresolved, with the latest dispute in the jury room adding to the possibility of a mistrial in a closely watched trial centred on Clancy's mental state and legal responsibility for the deaths of her three children.

The defense attorney for Lindsay Clancy, the woman accused of killing her three young children, has asked the judge to dismiss the lone holdout juror, who he claims “refuses to listen” to the rule on reasonable doubt.
Massachusetts Superior Court Judge William Sullivan sent jurors home on their sixth day of deliberations after speaking with each juror individually. Clancy’s defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, then addressed the judge and asked for the holdout juror to be ejected.

Reddington said the foreperson had brought the juror to the judge’s attention, saying he or she “refuses to listen to the law that you’ve given him or her unreasonable doubt.” The lawyer then said the judge’s asking jurors if they can “listen to the law as I instruct you” is not a sufficient question to remove the problem juror.
“It does not allow any foundation for a motion to remove the juror who refuses to accept your instructions on the law on reasonable doubt, and if we come back here in a half an hour with a mistrial because of a juror that has just spurned the instructions of this court, it’s a shame,” Reddington said. “It’s a real shame, and that’s why I object to the court’s ruling.”
The prosecution then told Sullivan it had no issue with the judge’s questions.
Sullivan then said dismissing a juror is a “sensitive undertaking,” adding that he will take in Reddington’s objection.
“I don’t feel it’s appropriate for me to say I agree with one juror or the left,” Sullivan said. “At this point, I’ve asked if they are able to follow my instructions, according they swore earlier that they could. They’ve said at this point that they can.”
Former federal prosecutor Neama Rahmani told the Washington Examiner that Reddington’s remarks may suggest he wants to remove the one juror who has sided with the prosecution.
“The reason Reddington went crazy, he thinks he can get a not criminally responsible. He smells blood in the water,” Rahmani said.
Rahmani added that a juror not following the rule on reasonable doubt could also indicate where the jury’s head is, and Reddington recognizes that.
“There’s one juror that’s not following the law on reasonable doubt,” Rahmani said. “Reasonable doubt helps the defense. Reddington goes crazy, tries to remove the juror. The judge says no. He senses a defense verdict, which is why he did what he did.”
Jurors will return Friday morning for their seventh day of deliberations. Based on Thursday’s conversations, it appears jurors are deadlocked 11-1. The jury is comprised of nine women and three men.

Clancy is accused of strangling her three children in their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in 2023 using exercise resistance bands. Clancy’s lawyers do not deny the murders but are seeking an insanity defense for Clancy, arguing that she was in a postpartum psychotic state when she committed the crime.
Clancy faces up to life in prison if the jury finds her guilty. However, if the jury finds Clancy not guilty on insanity grounds, she would be admitted into a state mental health institution.
Kaelan Deese contributed to this report.

The lead defense attorney for Lindsay Clancy on Thursday asked for a juror to be removed after the jury foreman said that individual appeared to cause the deadlock that has prevented the jury from reaching a verdict in the murder trial two times now.
Massachusetts Superior Court Judge William Sullivan denied the lawyer’s request to remove the juror and sent the jury back to continue deliberating, per The New York Times. The judge later ended deliberations for the day.
After reaching a deadlock two times, the jurors in the murder trial have one more chance to reach a verdict before the judge is able to declare a mistrial. The jury is made up of nine women and three men who got the case a week ago and have been deadlocked since at least Tuesday morning. Sullivan has continued to encourage them to try to reach a unanimous decision to avoid a mistrial.
On Thursday, the jury submitted a question to Sullivan. The judge then read out an explanation to the jury defining “proof beyond a reasonable doubt.”
“A charge is proved beyond a doubt if, after you’ve compared and considered all of the evidence, you have in your minds an abiding conviction to a moral certainty that the charge is true,” Sullivan said, per NBC News.
The judge added that it’s not enough to establish a strong probability that the defendant is “more likely guilty than not guilty.”
When the jurors were sent to resume deliberations, defense attorney Kevin Reddington told Sullivan that one juror was refusing to “listen to the law” and asked for the person to be removed. He said that the individual was ignoring the judge’s instructions around the standard of reasonable doubt, per CNN.
“I don’t feel that it is proper for me to side with one side or the other of the deliberations. I don’t feel it’s appropriate for me to say I agree with one juror or the 11,” Sullivan said as he declined the request, per NBC News.
The judge shared that each juror was brought in individually and questioned about whether they could follow his instructions. He added that each juror said they can at this point.
Jennifer Sprague, a prosecutor in the case, added that there is “no way to determine” how the deliberations are unfolding, in response to Reddington’s request to remove a juror.
Clancy has been accused of murder after strangling her three young children in 2023, per CNN. The prosecution argues that the Massachusetts mother acted “intentionally, rationally and swiftly” to murder her children, while the defense says she should not be held criminally responsible since she was suffering from postpartum psychosis.

Lone juror blocking verdict in US mother's child murder trial: defense
Plymouth (United States) (AFP) – The defense for Lindsay Clancy, the US mother accused of murdering her three children, on Thursday accused a single holdout juror of blocking a verdict in the high-profile trial.
Issued on:
Clancy, 36, does not deny strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, but claims she was suffering from postpartum psychosis -- excusing her from criminal responsibility.
Her five-week trial, which was televised and featured more than 80 witnesses, has sparked debate in the United States over maternal mental health.
Kevin Reddington, Clancy's main lawyer, told a Massachusetts court Thursday that there is "one juror who refuses to listen to the law that you've given him or her on reasonable doubt."
He requested that the juror be removed from the 12-member panel, but Judge William Sullivan refused and instead sent them back to continue a seventh day of deliberations Friday.
To reach a verdict, all 12 jurors must be in agreement.
If they cannot agree, the judge will declare a mistrial and prosecutors must decide whether to try the case again with a new jury.
On Wednesday, Sullivan issued the jurors a last-resort, so-called "dynamite charge" that encourages them to keep discussing in a bid to break the impasse and avoid a mistrial.
Clancy has pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, saying she heard a voice ordering her to kill her children. Her lawyers say this was caused by postpartum psychosis.
After the killings at her family home in Duxbury, Massachusetts in January 2023, she jumped from a second-story window in an apparent suicide attempt that left her paralyzed from the waist down.
The former nurse faces life in prison without the possibility of parole if found guilty of first-degree murder.
Jurors can also find Clancy guilty of second-degree murder, manslaughter, or not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility -- a verdict that would see Clancy sent to a psychiatric facility.

A single juror in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial is preventing the jury from reaching a unanimous verdict, her lawyer said in court on Thursday, after deliberations stretched into a sixth day over whether to convict the Massachusetts woman of killing her three young children.
Defense attorney Kevin Reddington made that statement shortly after the jury sent Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Massachusetts, a note that prompted him to re-instruct jurors on what would constitute "reasonable doubt."
After the jury was sent back to continue deliberating, Reddington moved to have a holdout juror removed, saying a note from the jury's foreperson indicated "there's one juror who refuses to listen to the law that you've given him or her on reasonable doubt."
"If we come back here in half an hour with a mistrial because of a juror that has just spurned the instructions of this court, it's a shame," Reddington told the judge, who declined to remove the juror.
The jury sent Sullivan a note a day earlier that said, "After much deliberation, we are still unable to come to a unanimous decision." They sent a similar note on Tuesday. But on both days, the judge instructed them to continue deliberating.
Mistrial may be declared
If the jury does not reach a verdict and Sullivan declares a mistrial, prosecutors would need to decide whether to retry the case, which has included more than 80 witnesses and more than 300 exhibits.
Asked during a lunch break about his thoughts on the state of the deliberations, Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz told reporters outside the courthouse that "we'll hang on and find out."
On the question of whether prosecutors in his office would retry the case if it ended in a mistrial, Cruz said only: "I'll talk when this is all over."
Life in prison without parole if convicted
Clancy, 36, faces life in prison without parole if convicted of first-degree murder. If found not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, or reason of insanity, she could be committed to a state psychiatric hospital for evaluation.
She has admitted to strangling her three children to death on January 24, 2023, with exercise bands in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to take her own life, which left her paralyzed.
During the six-week trial, defense attorney Kevin Reddington sought to convince jurors that Clancy was in the midst of a psychotic episode when she killed Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan.
Testimony from family members, including Clancy's now ex-husband, Patrick, showed how she had struggled with her mental health in the months after the birth of her third child, repeatedly seeking treatment from healthcare providers who prescribed her a myriad of drugs.
Prosecutors do not dispute that Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital, had been dealing with mental health issues.
But they argued she was able to appreciate the wrongfulness of killing her children and intentionally chose to do so anyway, opting to kill them because she had decided to kill herself and was convinced they would suffer without her.
